Empirical Research Plan: “The Economic Impacts of New Unionization on Private-Sector Employers”

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

1. Identification Strategy
Identification device: Fuzzy Regression Discontinuity Design (FRD) at the 50 percent certification-election threshold, optionally embedded in an event-study DiD framework when multiple pre/post years are available.

Why FRD is appropriate
• Under U.S. labor law a union is certified if it receives strictly more than 50 percent of valid ballots.  
• Near 50 percent the assignment of “union certified” is as good as random; firms marginally above and below the cutoff are observationally similar except for a discrete jump in the probability of becoming unionized.  
• The discontinuity is “fuzzy” because a small number of winning elections do not translate into enduring collective-bargaining agreements and (rarely) unions can be formed after losing.  
• Local, non-parametric estimation around the cutoff provides internally valid causal effects of unionization on outcomes such as wages, employment, and productivity.

If yearly panel outcomes are available, we will difference outcomes relative to a pre-election baseline within the RD window (“RD-in-time”) to raise precision and remove any smooth pre-existing trends.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

2. Treatment and Control

Treatment variable  
Treated = 1 if the certification election resulted in a union victory (vote share ≥50 %).  
Encouragement variable / running variable = vote share minus 50 %.

Control group  
Firms whose pro-union vote share lies just below 50 % (e.g., 45–49.9 %) within an optimally chosen bandwidth provide the counterfactual.

Timing / key variation  
The cross-section is defined at the year of the election (t=0) and subsequent years t=+1, +2 … if panel data exist. The causal variation is the discontinuous jump in the probability of being unionized at the ballot share cutoff.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

3. Key Identifying Assumptions

A1. Continuity of potential outcomes. In the absence of union certification, expected outcomes (wages, employment, productivity) evolve smoothly through the 50 % vote-share threshold.  
Plausibility: Campaign dynamics and NLRB supervision limit firms’ ability to perfectly manipulate one or two votes. Empirically testable using covariate balance and density tests.

A2. No precise manipulation of the running variable.  
Plausibility: Ballots are secret and counted by the NLRB, making deliberate sorting unlikely. A McCrary (2008) density test will be run.

A3. Stable unit treatment value (SUTVA). One firm’s union status does not directly affect another’s outcomes within the estimation window.  
Plausibility: Given the localized nature of bargaining units, spillovers across firms in the short run are limited.

A4. First-stage relevance. Crossing 50 % must lead to a large increase in the probability of actual unionization.  
Plausibility: Certification is mechanical, but we will document the first-stage jump.

A5. Local independence of covariates. Other firm characteristics vary smoothly at the cutoff.  
Plausibility: Will be checked empirically.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

4. Threats to Identification & Mitigation

T1. Manipulation of vote counts or voter rolls.  
Mitigation: (i) McCrary density test; (ii) symmetry checks on pre-determined covariates (employment, industry, region); (iii) exclude elections with documented fraud charges.

T2. Imperfect compliance (fuzziness). Some certified unions fail to negotiate contracts; some losers later become unionized.  
Mitigation: Use FRD; estimate LATE as ratio of reduced-form outcome discontinuity to first-stage discontinuity. Sensitivity: restrict to elections with contract in place within two years.

T3. Differential attrition or data availability post election (e.g., failing firms disappear).  
Mitigation: (i) Use administrative employment/wage series that track even dissolved entities; (ii) bound estimates using Lee (2009) trimming; (iii) show robustness to inverse-probability weights.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

5. R Code Outline (executable)

```r
#############################################################
# 0. Packages
#############################################################
library(tidyverse)    # data wrangling
library(rdrobust)     # RD estimation
library(rddensity)    # McCrary test
# (optional) library(fixest) for DID within RD

#############################################################
# 1. Load and prepare data
#############################################################
df <- read_csv("nlrb_firm_level_1984_2001.csv") %>% 
  mutate(vote_share = votes_for / eligible_voters,
         running    = vote_share - 0.50,            # centered running var
         treated    = as.integer(vote_share >= 0.50))

# Create outcomes
df <- df %>% 
  mutate(log_wage   = log(avg_hourly_wage),
         log_empl   = log(employment),
         log_valuea = log(value_added))             # productivity proxy

#############################################################
# 2. Main fuzzy RD: effect on log wages
#############################################################
# Select MSE-optimal bandwidth endogenously
bw  <- rdbwselect(y = df$log_wage, x = df$running)$bws[1,1]

rd_main <- rdrobust(y = df$log_wage, x = df$running,
                    c = 0, fuzzy = df$treated, h = bw, p = 1)

summary(rd_main)

#############################################################
# 3. Covariate balance & density test
#############################################################
# Covariate balance: pre-election employment
rd_balance <- rdrobust(y = log(df$employment_pre), x = df$running,
                       c = 0, fuzzy = df$treated)
summary(rd_balance)

# McCrary manipulation test
density_test <- rddensity(x = df$running, c = 0)
summary(density_test)

#############################################################
# 4. Robustness: alternative bandwidth (±10 pp) and polynomial (p=2)
#############################################################
alt   <- rdrobust(y = df$log_wage, x = df$running,
                  c = 0, fuzzy = df$treated, h = 0.10, p = 2)
summary(alt)
```

Optional: Panel DiD-within-RD

```r
# Keep ±10 pp window and create post indicator
panel <- df %>% 
  filter(abs(running) <= .10) %>% 
  mutate(post = year >= election_year)

fe <- fixest::feols(log_wage ~ treated*post | firm_id + year, data = panel,
                    cluster = ~firm_id)
summary(fe)
```

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

6. Expected Results (Priors)

• Wages: positive jump around 5–10 percent (consistent with union wage premium estimates).  
• Employment: modest decline, perhaps −2 % to −4 %, reflecting potential labor-demand response.  
• Productivity: ambiguous; theory predicts either slight increase via “voice” effects or slight decline via restrictive work rules. I expect a small positive (≤2 %) or near-zero effect.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (1 = clearly satisfied, 0 = questionable)

1. No manipulation of running variable (density test) ………………… 0.9  
2. Covariate balance around cutoff ……………………………………… 0.9  
3. Strong first stage (large jump in union status) …………………… 1.0  
4. Correct bandwidth / functional form chosen ……………………… 0.8  
5. No interference (SUTVA) / minimal spillovers ……………………… 0.8  

Average = 0.88 → Overall credibility high for local causal effects.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
